title: Serve with gladness (Psalm 100)
hookLine: a thanksgiving psalm said on weekdays: "Serve the LORD with gladness"
carry: thanks is the part meant to last
last: MAKE KNOWN HIS DOINGS AMONG THE PEOPLES.

lines: TWO WAYS TO WASH THE DISHES.
cards: There are two ways to wash the dishes. One with a sigh, scraping plates and counting the minutes. One with music on, maybe humming, warm water on your hands.
Same dishes, same time, a completely different hour of your life. The difference isn't the task; it's the gladness you bring.
Among the verses of song is a psalm only five verses long, and in its second verse it puts two words side by side, serve and gladness, as if they belong together.

teach.h: MIZMOR L'TODAH: A PSALM OF THANKS.
teach.b: Psalm one hundred has a heading, in the old Jewish translation: "A Psalm of thanksgiving." In Hebrew, mizmor l'todah.
A todah was a particular Temple offering, the thanksgiving offering, brought by someone who'd come through danger: a journey, an illness, a prison.
Then the psalm: "Shout unto the LORD, all the earth. Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing."
The Hebrew for serve, ivdu, shares its root with avodah, the word from the service of the heart, which means both work and worship. The same word for hauling stones and for prayer.
The psalm says: do it with simchah, with joy. Now the surprise.
In the Ashkenazi custom, this psalm is said on weekdays but skipped on Shabbat and festivals, because the thanksgiving offering, a personal, voluntary gift, wasn't brought on those days.
It's skipped too before Passover and through the festival, because the thanksgiving offering included loaves of leavened bread. The prayer book remembers the Temple calendar even here.
And a midrash says that in the time to come, all the offerings will cease except the thanksgiving offering, and all prayers will cease except the prayer of thanks.
Some teachers say that's why this psalm should be said with real joy, even sung. Of everything in the service, thanks is the part meant to last.

how: In the Ashkenazi rite, Psalm 100 is said in the weekday verses of song, often while standing and with joy, and is left out on Shabbat, festivals, the eve of Passover, the intermediate days of Passover and the eve of Yom Kippur.

o: rest: a day set apart from all labor
service: work and worship in one word

s: in the Ashkenazi custom Psalm 100 is said every day of the year
it's skipped on Shabbat and festivals, when the thanksgiving offering wasn't brought.
the Hebrew for serve shares a root with the word for worship
avodah means both work and worship.
a midrash says the thanksgiving offering is the one that will never cease
in the time to come, all offerings cease except thanks.

games.q: it's Passover week. the prayer book reaches Psalm 100, the psalm of the thanksgiving offering. what happens?
games.why: it's skipped in the Ashkenazi custom: the thanksgiving offering included leavened loaves, which aren't eaten on Passover.

practice: Pick one chore waiting for you, dishes, email, laundry, the commute, and picture doing it the sighing way, noticing how it feels in your chest.

Then picture it again, slower, with a song, with attention to the warm water or the sunlight through the bus window, and notice what changes. If you pray, you can say ivdu et Hashem b'simchah, serve the LORD with gladness.

wordCard.voice: Avodah, the Hebrew word for service, work and worship together, the root shared by Psalm one hundred's call to serve the Lord with gladness.

carryVoice: Your line: thanks is the part meant to last. Work and worship share one word. Day five hundred fifty-six, done.
